about.heading: About me
paragraphs: I am a software engineer who is passionate about creating elegant, efficient, and user-friendly web applications. With over 5 years of experience in the industry, I have developed a strong foundation in various programming languages, frameworks, and tools. Angular is my main subject in enterprise work; React and Next.js are what I use for my freelance clients.

I've always loved computers and tinkering with them, which led me to discover my passion for programming and coding. Despite studying Electrical and Electronic Engineering, I never lost sight of this passion and decided to pursue a career in software engineering to combine my academic background with my creative and technical interests.

When I'm not coding, you'll likely find me out on a run or hitting the gym. I believe that regular exercise is not only essential for physical health, but also for mental clarity, stress relief, and overall well-being.

projects.name: Portfolio & CV ecosystem
projects.description: This site and my online CV, built as one system: a single content source feeds both, so a text or theme change publishes everywhere without touching either app.
highlights: Standalone components and signals; content and design tokens fetched at runtime from the CV repo.
Zero content in the app repo, so copy changes never require a frontend deploy.
Deployed by GitHub Actions on every push.

caseStudy.headline: Portfolio and online CV built as one system, so a wording or theme change publishes to both without a frontend deploy.
caseStudy.context: I keep a public portfolio and an online CV. Maintained separately, the two drift: a job changes, one gets updated, the other quietly goes stale. I rebuilt them in 2026 as one system with a single content source.
caseStudy.goal: One place to change text or visual style, with the change appearing on both surfaces.
caseStudy.role: Sole author: the content model, the Angular application, the shared design tokens and the deployment.
approach: Standalone components and signals; content and design tokens fetched at runtime from the CV repo.
Zero content in the app repo, so copy changes never require a frontend deploy.
Deployed by GitHub Actions on every push.
results: A wording change is an edit to one content file; the portfolio picks it up on the next page load, with no frontend release.
Design tokens are published alongside the content, so both sites share one palette by construction.
Every push deploys through GitHub Actions; there is no manual release step.

projects.name: CV generator with automated A4 PDF
projects.description: A static-site generator that turns one content file into an online CV, a true-A4 print page and a downloadable PDF, so the published PDF can never drift from the site.
highlights: Content lives in plain key/value files and is validated against per-field length limits, failing the build when copy would break the layout.
Print stylesheet renders real 210mm A4 rather than relying on the browser's shrink-to-fit.
The PDF is generated by headless Chrome during the build and published with the site.

caseStudy.headline: One content source builds the online CV, a true-A4 print page and the downloadable PDF, so the PDF cannot go stale.
caseStudy.context: Keeping an online CV and a PDF in sync by hand fails quietly: the page gets edited, the PDF does not, and the version people receive stops matching the one on the web.
caseStudy.goal: Generate every output from one content source, and make the printed page a real A4 document rather than a browser page squeezed onto paper.
caseStudy.role: Sole author: the content model and its validation, the SCSS and print stylesheet, the Node build, the tests and the CI pipeline.
approach: Content lives in plain key/value files and is validated against per-field length limits, failing the build when copy would break the layout.
Print stylesheet renders real 210mm A4 rather than relying on the browser's shrink-to-fit.
The PDF is generated by headless Chrome during the build and published with the site.
results: The site, the print page and the PDF are generated from the same content, so the download always matches what is published.
Copy that would overflow the layout fails the build instead of shipping, thanks to per-field length limits.
The print stylesheet targets real 210mm A4, so the PDF is a proper document rather than a scaled-down screen layout.

projects.name: CoachingSeafarers
projects.description: Marketing site and lead funnel for a maritime leadership coach, built on Next.js with server-side form handling and no third-party tracking.
highlights: Two conversion paths on one site: a free five-day email mini-course as the entry point, and an application form for the paid coaching programme.
Forms run through Next.js Server Actions, so the email and CRM integration never appears in the client bundle.
Custom Tailwind palette and self-hosted fonts through next/font, with next/image serving WebP and preloading the hero.
Structured data for both the practice and the FAQ, full Open Graph metadata, and PWA scaffolding.
No analytics, chat widgets or trackers of any kind, so there is no cookie banner and nothing slowing the page down.
Search indexing deliberately disabled at the client's request: the practice is reached through LinkedIn and WhatsApp rather than organic search.

caseStudy.headline: A lead funnel for a maritime coaching practice: free mini-course in, coaching applications out, with no tracking scripts in between.
caseStudy.context: A Master Mariner running a coaching practice for senior deck officers needed a site that could qualify the right clients rather than collect everyone. The audience is at sea, often on poor connections.
caseStudy.goal: Turn visitors into two clearly separated funnels — a free mini-course for people exploring, and a gated application for people ready to commit — on a site that loads fast anywhere.
caseStudy.role: Freelance engagement: built and delivered the site.
challenges: The audience reads the site from ships, so page weight and render speed matter more than usual; every third-party script was a cost the site could not justify.
Two funnels on one page must not compete: the free offer has to be easy to take without cannibalising the paid application.
Handling form submissions without exposing the email or CRM provider to the browser.
A coaching practice carries a legal line between coaching and therapy that the copy and structure have to respect consistently.
The client did not want the practice discoverable through search, so the site had to convert visitors who arrive from a direct referral rather than rely on organic traffic.
approach: Two conversion paths on one site: a free five-day email mini-course as the entry point, and an application form for the paid coaching programme.
Forms run through Next.js Server Actions, so the email and CRM integration never appears in the client bundle.
Custom Tailwind palette and self-hosted fonts through next/font, with next/image serving WebP and preloading the hero.
Structured data for both the practice and the FAQ, full Open Graph metadata, and PWA scaffolding.
No analytics, chat widgets or trackers of any kind, so there is no cookie banner and nothing slowing the page down.
Search indexing deliberately disabled at the client's request: the practice is reached through LinkedIn and WhatsApp rather than organic search.
results: The site is live and serving both funnels: mini-course signup and coaching application, each with its own confirmation page.
Zero third-party scripts, so no cookie banner is needed and there is nothing between the visitor and the content.
Statically prerendered and served from Vercel's edge, with the hero image preloaded as WebP.

caseStudy.headline: A booking site for licence-free boat rentals, with a private installable route guide for customers once they are on the water.
caseStudy.context: The business rents small boats that need no licence, on Salamina. Customers are day trippers who want to know where they can actually go before they commit, and then need guidance once they are out at sea.

The route guide is for customers only, which means a gate that is simple enough for a holidaymaker on a phone at the dock.
Guidance is consumed at sea, where connectivity is unreliable — hence an installable app rather than a web page to load on the spot.

Nutrition data is personal, so storage and access rules carry real weight.

projects.name: Real-Time Voice AI Platform
projects.description: A real-time conversational voice AI platform designed for low-latency, interruption-aware and safety-controlled voice interactions.
highlights: Core C++ audio primitives: PCM validation, audio frame handling, jitter buffering and fixed-capacity SPSC queues.
A working TCP/WebSocket listener feeding incoming PCM audio into the real-time processing path.
Deterministic ASR and TTS test doubles, so the pipeline can be exercised without waiting on model integrations.
Bounded per-producer media queues built around single-producer, single-consumer ownership.
An engineering workflow of small tickets, explicit invariants and automated validation, so implementation status is evidence-based.

caseStudy.headline: Conversational voice treated as a real-time system rather than a sequential speech pipeline — bounded memory, predictable execution, and interruption handled at the audio layer.
caseStudy.context: The project explores how conversational voice AI can operate as a real-time system rather than a conventional sequential speech pipeline. The current implementation focuses on establishing reliable low-level audio transport, bounded concurrency and testable runtime foundations.
caseStudy.goal: Build and validate the technical foundations for a responsive real-time voice system, keeping latency, memory ownership, interruption handling and system safety explicit architectural concerns.
caseStudy.role: Freelance engagement: designed the system architecture, engineering constraints and validation approach, and contributed to the real-time C++ prototype.
challenges: Designing the audio path around bounded memory and predictable execution needed deliberate ownership, queueing and concurrency decisions rather than generic application patterns.
Real-time interruption and streaming behaviour has to be coordinated across audio transport, session state and generation boundaries, without letting stale work reach playback.
Probabilistic model output and deterministic control are separated by design, so actions and critical values pass a validation boundary before they take effect.
approach: Core C++ audio primitives: PCM validation, audio frame handling, jitter buffering and fixed-capacity SPSC queues.
A working TCP/WebSocket listener feeding incoming PCM audio into the real-time processing path.
Deterministic ASR and TTS test doubles, so the pipeline can be exercised without waiting on model integrations.
Bounded per-producer media queues built around single-producer, single-consumer ownership.
An engineering workflow of small tickets, explicit invariants and automated validation, so implementation status is evidence-based.
results: A reproducible local real-time prototype, with unit and end-to-end validation passing at the recorded implementation snapshot.
Network ingress verified over real loopback, from gateway through to audio processing.
Deterministic ASR and TTS pipeline behaviour and bounded media-queue operation verified by automated tests.

projects.name: Premium Culinary Creator Platform
projects.description: A subscription platform where culinary creators publish recipes and service proposals, with a ledgered points economy, rankings and Stripe billing.
highlights: Votes are an immutable ledger with a rebuildable aggregate: the vote, the voter's debit, the aggregate update and the credit to the recipe owner all commit in one transaction, or none of them do.

Subscription entitlements resolve through a single config-driven service, with a database-level invariant that a profile can hold only one active package at a time and package switches preserve history.
Media lives in a private object store, uploaded and displayed through presigned URLs so files are never public and never pass through the app server.
Domain logic sits in a service layer with thin API route handlers, so the same backend can serve a mobile client later without a rewrite.
One responsive app from phone to desktop rather than separate mobile and desktop builds.

caseStudy.headline: A creator platform where votes cost real balance — so every rule about money, entitlements and voting had to hold under concurrency, not just in the happy path.
caseStudy.context: Culinary creators publish recipes and service proposals to a paying audience. Readers spend a voting balance to back what they like, creators earn from being backed, and what each side may do depends on the package they hold — so the product is a content platform and a small economy at the same time.
caseStudy.goal: Ship an engineering MVP where the money paths are provably correct: subscriptions, entitlements, wallets and voting all enforced server-side, with the rules in configuration rather than scattered through the code.
caseStudy.role: Freelance engagement: built the platform end to end — data model, service layer, interface, payments and the verification tooling.
challenges: A vote spends balance, so it is a financial transaction, not a click: insufficient balance has to reject cleanly and two simultaneous votes on the same key must not both succeed.
Entitlements are sold, so what the interface offers and what the server enforces cannot drift apart — every displayed benefit needs a real server-side implementation behind it.
Billing arrives asynchronously by webhook, which has to be signature-checked, deduplicated and able to revoke access when a payment is disputed.
A schema this size only stays trustworthy if the migration chain reproduces the deployed database exactly, rather than being patched by hand along the way.
approach: Votes are an immutable ledger with a rebuildable aggregate: the vote, the voter's debit, the aggregate update and the credit to the recipe owner all commit in one transaction, or none of them do.

Subscription entitlements resolve through a single config-driven service, with a database-level invariant that a profile can hold only one active package at a time and package switches preserve history.
Media lives in a private object store, uploaded and displayed through presigned URLs so files are never public and never pass through the app server.
Domain logic sits in a service layer with thin API route handlers, so the same backend can serve a mobile client later without a rewrite.
One responsive app from phone to desktop rather than separate mobile and desktop builds.
results: 434 automated tests across 54 files, with typecheck, lint, test and build all green.

17 standalone verification scripts covering the paths where correctness is money: voting concurrency, wallet ledger, entitlements, the single-active-subscription invariant, webhook signature and dedupe, and reward redemption.
The migration chain is proven to reproduce the deployed schema exactly, with zero drift.
183 commits over roughly two weeks, from empty repository to a complete engineering MVP.

caseStudy.headline: Moving a large-scale eBanking platform off legacy AngularJS and onto the current Angular ecosystem, while it stays in production.
caseStudy.context: The platform covers the journeys an eBanking product is expected to have: payments, transfers, approvals and multi-step transactional flows. A large part of it was written in AngularJS and is being brought onto the current Angular ecosystem, with a design refresh landing alongside. Customers keep using the product throughout.
caseStudy.goal: Carry the existing behaviour onto modern Angular without interrupting the product, and deliver the rebrand in the same pass.
caseStudy.role: Angular Developer / Full Stack at 1DataGroup Technologies, working primarily on the Angular side and on the .NET BFF that serves it. The work is ongoing.
approach: Complex banking workflows: payments, transfers, approvals and multi-step transactional journeys.
Figma designs translated into responsive, production-ready interfaces supporting a rebrand.
Unit testing, release processes and pipeline work alongside feature delivery.
results: Banking journeys are moving onto modern Angular one flow at a time, with the platform staying available to customers throughout.
The system runs in production and is in use today.
challenges: AngularJS and modern Angular do not map one to one. Scopes, two-way binding and the old dependency injection style have no direct equivalent, so each screen is re-expressed rather than translated, and the business logic has to survive that rewrite intact.
The two generations coexist while the migration is in flight, which constrains routing, shared state and the build setup for as long as both are live.

Banking flows leave no room for approximation. A transfer, an approval or a multi-step journey either behaves exactly as before or it is a defect, so parity has to be demonstrated rather than assumed.
A rebrand running in parallel means design changes and logic migration have to advance without blocking each other.

approach: Migrated legacy patterns to standalone components and modern Angular APIs.
Adopted Signals for state and data flow, improving change-detection efficiency.
Kept feature parity through incremental migration and regression checks.
results: Delivered for a fixed election date with feature parity preserved, through incremental migration steps and regression checks.
Standalone components and Signals replaced the legacy patterns, simplifying state flow and change detection.
Project structure and tooling aligned with current Angular standards, so the application is back on a supported version with a maintainable upgrade path.
The system runs in production and is in use today.
challenges: Eleven major framework versions in one move: the rendering engine, the module system and a long tail of deprecated APIs all change at once, so there is no small incremental step available.
Third-party libraries pinned to the old version have to be upgraded or replaced in lockstep, and every replacement is a behavioural risk of its own.
Major RxJS and TypeScript upgrades ride along with the framework, touching code that has nothing to do with the migration itself.
The output is published numbers, so a state or rendering bug is not cosmetic — feature parity had to hold under a deadline that could not absorb a slip.

Delivered two brands from one shared codebase: roughly 90% common functionality with one or two brand-specific features and a distinct UI each.

A points programme has two very different audiences in the same product — customers and operators — with different permissions and different expectations of the same data.
